extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity professionals, science journalists, and interested science readers
extracted.subtask_description: Judging how researchers correct the scientific record and how replication attempts should be evaluated — including what counts as a true replication, how retractions should be marked, and norms for public responses. Useful for assessing integrity and methodological comparability in empirical research (illustrated here with a psychology case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging retracted publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should clearly indicate when a listed publication has been retracted (e.g., marking it as 'RETRACTED' in their list of publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A retracted paper should be plainly and unambiguously flagged on CVs, personal websites, and publication lists so readers are immediately aware (the post notes Hauser later showed the retraction notice in red with the word RETRACTED).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections should be factual and not self-justifying
rubrics_metrics.description: When correcting the record, the correction should state the facts; adding self-serving commentary (e.g., 'but I was right!') undermines the purpose of a correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep public corrections neutral and focused on the factual status of the work. Avoid using correction notices or public acknowledgements to defend prior conduct or to conflate separate debates (the post criticizes Hauser for appending a 'but I was right' tone).

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a valid replication
rubrics_metrics.description: A replication must use comparable methods, materials, sample characteristics, and presentation to the original study; substantial methodological differences mean the study is not a true replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key factors to match/include: sample size and power, subject population/demographics, testing environment (e.g., anonymous web vs. in-person with experimenter), exact stimuli/wording, presence/absence of diagrams or other aids, and scenario variants. If these differ, conflicting results may reflect methodological differences rather than failure to replicate (as Hauser argues regarding Greene et al. and Waldmann & Dieterich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting failures to replicate (consider confounds and methodological differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to replicate should be interpreted in light of methodological differences and potential confounds (e.g., wording differences that change participants' interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before concluding that an effect is non-robust, examine whether differences in design, wording, presentation, or sampling could explain divergent outcomes; test those differences explicitly. Alternative explanations should be considered and reported (the post cites claims that wording confounds account for prior differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific credibility depends on honesty and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific enterprise relies on honesty; researchers found to be untrustworthy may have their work—and future outputs—disregarded by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical conduct and transparency are foundational. When misconduct is established, readers and colleagues may appropriately question or discount the individual's contributions until trust is rebuilt or independently verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate theoretical/speculative claims from empirical results where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: To preserve defensible theoretical contributions when empirical results are questioned, authors may consider publishing theoretical exposition separately from empirical datasets/results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As suggested in commentary, splitting a manuscript into a theoretical paper and a data/results paper can allow retraction of problematic empirical work while retaining the theoretical discussion, provided the theory is clearly labeled as speculation and distinct from the (retracted) data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations for oversight and investigative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative agencies and institutional processes (e.g., ORI) should operate competently, transparently, and in accordance with regulations; their findings will be scrutinized and may be controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should follow established rules, provide appropriate expertise, protect procedural fairness, and be open to scrutiny. Critics may point to perceived incompetence or lack of transparency; defenders note the need to comply with regulations and protect parties during inquiry (as debated in comments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting and responding to alleged failed replications
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleged replication failures are publicized (e.g., on replication registries or blogs), authors should document methodological differences and, where needed, publicly respond with specific, testable claims about why the studies differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use replication tracking resources (e.g., psychfiledrawer) to locate attempts; respond with detailed, evidence-based replies that identify precise methodological differences and suggest how to test whether those differences account for divergent results (Hauser posted point-by-point methodological comparisons in his reply).
